newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM says Pol Pot kills aide, on the run.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM says Pol Pot kills aide, on the run.

text.p: Ailing Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot killed his defence chief and 11 members of his family and fled his northern stronghold with the Maoist movement's nominal leader as hostage, Cambodia's co-premier said on Friday.

The ageing Pol Pot, who led the Khmer Rouge during its brutal "killing fields" rule over Cambodia from 1975 to early 1979, was carried away by his men in a sling, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters.

"Mr Pol Pot had accused (defence chief) Son Sen of being allied with Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, so on the 10th of June at 2 a.m., he killed Son Sen and 11 of his family members very brutally, very cruelly, by shooting them and running over the dead with a truck," said Ranariddh.
Pol Pot then fled the guerrillas' Anlong Veng base along with 200 of his hardline loyalists, taking along Khieu Samphan, who has been the group's nominal leader, as hostage.
Ranariddh's announcement came amid persistent reports in recent days of conflict between Pol Pot, Son Sen and Khieu Samphan.
The conflict mirrored growing differences between Cambodia's two premiers, Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy alliance after May 1993 United Nations-sponsored elections.

"The day before yesterday he (Pol Pot) arrested Khieu Samphan and escaped Anlong Veng with 200 troops. Pol Pot is ill, he could not walk by himself, but he was carried by his men with a sling," Ranariddh said.
He did not say where Pol Pot had gone.
Ranariddh said about 95 percent of an estimated 2,000 Khmer Rouge guerrillas had defected to the Cambodian government and troops were moving in to try to trap Pol Pot.
Cambodia had sealed off its northern border in reaction to the news about Pol Pot, he added. Thailand also said it would help search for Pol Pot and seal its side of the border.
Clandestine Khmer Rouge Radio, which normally broadcasts news in the morning, was silent on Friday morning.
Pol Pot was rumoured earlier this week to have left Cambodia for Bangkok en route to political exile in China. Thai military sources and China denied this.
During the Khmer Rouge's iron-fisted rule, more than one million people died in Cambodia from executions, starvation, overwork or sickness.

The Khmer Rouge has been badly split since thousands of the guerrillas started defecting in mid-1996 to the Cambodian government side. Most prominent among the defectors was Ieng Sary, former foreign minister and Pol Pot's brother-in-law.
Ranariddh said he had photographs of the bodies of Son Sen and members of his family but did not say when he would release them.
"I have enough evidence with pictures to show the killing of Son Sen," the premier said.

Ranariddh did not say where or how he obtained the news of Son Sen's death and photographs. But one of his senior military commanders returned on Thursday night from a one-day trip to Anlong Veng where he was said to have met Khmer Rouge hardliners.
"I hope this is the end of the life of the Khmer Rouge really because Pol Pot cannot live any longer," he said.
Ranariddh said he had no information on the group's army commander, the one-legged Ta Mok.
"I would like to inform you that Khmer Rouge problems in Anlong Veng are reaching a level of complexity that we cannot understand," he added.
Ranariddh said his senior army commanders had asked for more arms to equip Khmer Rouge defectors to fight Pol Pot and he had approved the request.
In Bangkok, a senior Thai general said Thailand would seal off the northern Thai-Cambodian border and cooperate with the Cambodian government to capture Pol Pot.

"The immediate task for the Cambodian troops is to rescue Khieu Samphan and later join hands in crushing the remaining Khmer Rouge guerrillas led by the hardliner Pol Pot," the general who deals with the Cambodian conflict told Reuters.

"Pol Pot would have no where to go but to die in Cambodia," the general said, adding that Pol Pot's actions in killing his defence minister Son Sen and abducting nominal leader Khieu Samphan were unforgivable acts.
